prompt.context: Our client, UK-based Magic Media, is participating in an auction for the rights to broadcast the 2016 Quiddich World Cup. Magic Media is a mature company that derives the vast majority of its revenues from selling TV advertisements.
prompt.question: What should we bid on the broadcasting rights? What factors will affect our bid?

clarifying_info.q: Who are our competitors in the auction?
clarifying_info.a: Magic Media has 3 competitors: 2 smaller US-based players looking to boost their international presence (likely higher production costs, possibly lower ad revenues, may be willing to loss-lead), and 1 large UK-based competitor that is a mature company with similar economics to Magic Media.

clarifying_info.q: How long does the World Cup last and what is the broadcast schedule?
clarifying_info.a: The tournament lasts 3 weeks (21 days). It begins with an opening ceremony on a Sunday afternoon and ends with the final match and closing ceremony on a Saturday evening. We can broadcast 6 hours per weekday and 8 hours per weekend day. We can broadcast an extra 2 hours on ceremony days.
Heavier viewing is expected during weekday evenings (the last 2 hours of each weekday), all weekend days, and peak viewing during the final day of games and the two ceremonies.
Due to the complicated logistics of the event, we will need to spend an extra $10M to produce the broadcast over our normal programming.

We can show ads for no more than 10 minutes per hour. We charge double our normal rates: $50K/min for non-prime time, $200K/min for prime time, and $500K/min for peak (normally $25K/min, $100K/min and $250K/min respectively).

clarifying_info.q: When does the auction take place relative to the World Cup?
clarifying_info.a: The auction is happening now (2011) and the World Cup takes place in 2016, so there is a 5-year gap between payment and receipt of advertising revenues.

framework: Determine total marginal TV revenue from broadcasting the World Cup
Classify broadcast hours into peak, prime, and non-prime categories and calculate ad revenue for each
Subtract incremental production costs to get marginal profit
Discount marginal profit back to present value using an appropriate cost of capital (5-year delay between payment and revenue)
Analyze competitor bidding dynamics: UK competitor has similar economics; US competitors may loss-lead; set bid strategy accordingly

questions.prompt: Calculate the total number of peak, prime, and non-prime broadcast hours over the tournament.
questions.guidance: Tournament = 21 days total: 15 weekdays, 5 normal weekend days, 1 final match day. Weekdays: 6 hrs each, last 2 hrs = prime (30 prime hrs), first 4 hrs = non-prime (60 non-prime hrs). Weekend days (5): 8 hrs each = 40 prime hrs. Final match day + opening ceremony day + closing ceremony day = 3 ceremony/final days, each with 2 extra hours = 6 extra hours, but opening is Sunday (a weekend) and closing is Saturday (a weekend); the final match day also involves ceremony hours. Total peak = final match day hours + opening ceremony hours + closing ceremony hours = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 peak hours. Prime = 30 (weekday evenings) + 40 (regular weekends) = 70 prime hours. Non-prime = 60 hours (weekday non-evening).

math.setup: 21-day tournament: 15 weekdays (6 hrs/day), 5 regular weekend days (8 hrs/day), 1 final match day (8+2=10 hrs, counted as peak). Opening ceremony (Sunday, 8+2=10 hrs peak) and closing ceremony (Saturday, 8+2=10 hrs peak).
steps: Peak hours: opening ceremony day (Sunday) + closing ceremony/final match day (Saturday) + final match day itself; casebook treats these as 3 special days each contributing ~4 hrs peak = 12 peak hours
Prime hours: 2 prime hrs/weekday × 15 weekdays = 30; 8 hrs × 5 regular weekend days = 40; total prime = 70 hours
Non-prime hours: 4 non-prime hrs/weekday × 15 weekdays = 60 hours
math.answer: 12 peak hours, 70 prime hours, 60 non-prime hours

questions.prompt: Calculate the total advertising revenue from broadcasting the World Cup.
questions.guidance: Apply 10 min of ads per hour at the respective doubled rates for each category.

math.setup: Revenue = (peak hours × $500K/min × 10 min) + (prime hours × $200K/min × 10 min) + (non-prime hours × $50K/min × 10 min)

questions.prompt: Calculate marginal profit from broadcasting the World Cup.
questions.guidance: Magic Media already has existing programming that it displaces. The $230M is total revenue but half is the baseline (what they would have earned from normal programming at normal rates). The incremental revenue is $230M / 2 = $115M. Subtract extra production costs of $10M.

math.setup: Marginal profit = (Total revenue / 2) – Extra production costs

questions.prompt: The World Cup takes place in 2016 but the auction is this year (2011). How much is the future stream of revenue worth today?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the 5-year time delay and apply a present value discount. If candidate asks about interest rates, prompt them to make a reasoned assumption (10% is the guide answer). PV = $105M / (1.10)^5.

math.setup: PV = Marginal profits / (1 + cost of capital)^years = $105M / (1.10)^5

questions.prompt: Given the auction dynamics with 3 competitors, what should Magic Media bid?
questions.guidance: The UK competitor has similar economics, so their valuation should also be around $65.2M. US competitors may loss-lead (bid above intrinsic value for strategic reasons). Magic Media should bid close to but below $65.2M to capture some surplus; bidding at value ($65.2M) is also acceptable as it meets cost of capital. Key insight: underbidding is risky given uncertainty introduced by the US loss-leaders. Candidates should also note that extra viewership may spill over to normal programming, increasing marginal revenue by $2.5M–$10M.

brainstorming.prompt: What risks could affect our revenue projections or bidding strategy?

categories.name: Revenue risks
ideas: Insufficient advertiser demand to fill all time slots at the premium rates
Lower-than-expected viewership reducing ad rates or fill rates
Competing broadcasters undercutting ad prices if they also acquire partial rights

categories.name: Competitor bidding risks
ideas: UK competitor bids aggressively, forcing Magic Media into a winner's curse
US competitors loss-lead and win the rights, removing competitive threat
Insufficient intelligence on competitors' cost structures and willingness to pay

categories.name: Operational risks
ideas: Production costs exceed the $10M estimate due to logistics complexity
Technical failures during broadcast damaging brand and advertiser relationships
Currency risk given UK base but potentially USD-denominated costs

categories.name: Model assumption risks
ideas: Revenue model is too optimistic (e.g., peak/prime hour classification may differ)
Cost of capital assumption of 10% may understate or overstate the discount
Spill-over viewership to other programming hard to quantify and may not materialize

recommendation: Magic Media should bid below but close to the projected present value of $65.2M
A bid at value ($65.2M) is also acceptable as it produces profits meeting the cost of capital, but carries more risk if the model is too optimistic
risks: Revenue projections may not be met if advertiser demand for time slots is insufficient
The UK competitor may underbid to increase gains, creating strategic uncertainty
US competitors may loss-lead, creating upward pressure on the winning bid and potential winner's curse
Overall model assumptions (viewership, fill rates, cost of capital) could be too optimistic
next_steps: Research past bidding behavior of the UK competitor to assess their likely strategy
Gather more data on advertiser demand and willingness to pay at the doubled rates
Model downside scenarios to stress-test the $65.2M valuation before finalizing the bid
Assess whether spill-over viewership from the World Cup can be monetized on normal programming (adds $2.5M–$10M to value)
